Description: A short summary of the work. This helps users quickly understand the software's purpose.
The creators of the software. Each author can be an individual person or a group, such as a research institution or company.
The version of the Citation File Format standard used in this file. It ensures the file is interpreted correctly by tools.
The specific commit hash from the version control system for this version of the software. This provides a precise reference to the code.
The individuals or groups to contact for support or inquiries about the software. This helps direct communication to the right people.
The date when this version of the software was made publicly available. This corresponds to the Schema.org 'datePublished' property.
The Digital Object Identifier (DOI) for the software version. A DOI provides a persistent and unique link to the work.
A list of other unique identifiers for the software, such as a SWHID or an archive URL. This helps in uniquely identifying and locating the work.
A list of keywords or tags that describe the software. These help with discovery and categorization.
The license under which the software is provided, typically as a standard SPDX identifier. This informs users of the permissions and restrictions.
A URL pointing to the full text of the software's license. This provides users with the specific legal terms.
A required message for users, typically instructing them on how to cite the software. For example: "If you use this software, please cite it as below."
A specific reference that the authors prefer to be cited, such as a paper describing the software. This guides users to the most appropriate citation.
A list of relevant publications or other works related to the software. These could be papers that use, describe, or are built upon by the software.
The URL of a public repository where a version of the software is archived, such as on Zenodo or Figshare. This points to a citable, preserved copy.
The URL of a specific build or package of the software, such as a JAR file, container image, or wheel. This points to a runnable or installable version.
The URL of the source code repository for the software. This is typically a link to a platform like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket.
The official name of the software being cited. This serves as the primary human-readable identifier for the work.
The type of the work being cited, which must be 'software'. This clarifies the nature of the cited entity.
The URL of the software's project website or landing page. This provides a general entry point for information about the software.
The version number of the software being cited. This should ideally follow a standard like Semantic Versioning.
